summary: The machine already has the key runtime, the documentdb MCP data-plane server, the Learn documentation server, and the DocumentDB skills needed to build the Python LangChain sample against the provided live cluster. Most cold answers were either out-of-date or confused with Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) or older DocumentDB/Cosmos names; authoritative Microsoft docs are available to correct them. Missing developer conveniences (mongosh) and a few unspecified design choices (embedding model / dimensions, seed data, exact Python pinning, risk scoring formula) leave workable gaps the builder must resolve before finalizing the sample.
summary_points: All essential runtime/tools for the sample are available: Python, pip, Docker, Node/npx, az CLI, the documentdb MCP server (data-plane) and the Microsoft Learn doc search tool.
Several cold answers confused this service with Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) or older product names — critical corrections are documented and must be applied.
Vector search, hybrid (BM25+vector) search, and the recommended vector-index commands (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann with cosmosSearch) are documented and available on the cluster.
Billing for this service is vCore/compute-tier (M-series) + storage (not RU-based); the sample environment already uses an M30 cluster — adjust cost guidance accordingly.
Useful CLI tooling is missing: mongosh is not on PATH (recommended to add for manual debugging); azd/bicep/terraform/dotnet are not present but not required for this sample.

The builder must pick an embedding model and dimension, create seed data, and supply .env.example and pinned Python dependency constraints; these are information gaps not answered by the installed skills or docs.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child types include Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /collections for MongoDB API).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. The correct resource type for managed vCore DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not the Cosmos DB databaseAccounts resource).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) resource model used by the older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource; the newer/vCore offering uses a dedicated resource type named mongoClusters.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts as the resource type, IaC (Bicep/Terraform) would target the wrong resource and fail or create a different service (Cosmos DB account), causing deployment and configuration mismatches.
improvements: Add a prominent note on the DocumentDB quickstart pages clarifying that vCore DocumentDB clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts), with an example Bicep/ARM/Terraform snippet.
Update the agent kit's resource-type mapping to prefer `mongoClusters` for DocumentDB samples.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core Azure CLI group `az cosmosdb` (not an extra extension). Example: `az cosmosdb create ...`
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the `az documentdb mongocluster` command group to create/manage clusters (e.g., `az documentdb mongocluster create ...`). The command group is provided by the DocumentDB CLI extension/command set (`az documentdb`).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The `az cosmosdb` group is the historical CLI group for Cosmos DB accounts; the vCore DocumentDB service exposes `az documentdb mongocluster` commands.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would target the wrong control-plane API and not create/modify the expected mongoClusters resources; CLI scripts in the sample would fail.
improvements: Document the correct `az documentdb mongocluster` command in the sample README and include an example `az` snippet to list/create clusters.
Add a short migration note in CLI docs distinguishing `az documentdb` vs `az cosmosdb` usage.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@{apiVersion}; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account ... kind = 'MongoDB'.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore DocumentDB clusters use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (Bicep/ARM) or the equivalent AzAPI/Terraform resource targeting microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters; do not use the cosmos `databaseAccounts` resource for vCore clusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Mongo API uses databaseAccounts in templates; the newer vCore product has its own resource type `mongoClusters`.
confusions.build_risk: IaC snippets using databaseAccounts would not deploy the intended vCore cluster and would produce a mismatched service (or fail).
improvements: Add example Bicep and Terraform snippets using `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` to the sample's README.
Agent kit should include a template fragment for `mongoClusters` to avoid sample authors using `databaseAccounts` by habit.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos Mongo API connection: `mongodb://<user>:<pwd>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@` (port 10255, host `.mongo.cosmos.azure.com`).
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters the cluster exposes standard Mongo-style connection strings (often `mongodb+srv://` or `mongodb://`) with the cluster domain such as `*.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` (SRV form) or the explicit host and the provider-supplied port(s); the service provides `list-connection-strings` that return SCRAM-SHA-256 connection strings. Do not assume the older `.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255` form — use `az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings` or portal to get the canonical strings.

grounding_links.title: Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString-Description
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the classic Cosmos DB Mongo API host suffix and port (mongodb.cosmos.azure.com:10255). vCore cluster connection strings use different hostnames and SRV forms; the precise host/port should be read from cluster's list-connection-strings output.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding the old host/port and options may fail to connect or use wrong authentication mechanism; builder must fetch and use the cluster-provided connection string (from az or portal).
improvements: In the sample README instruct builders to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env and show `az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings` as the authoritative method to obtain the connection string.
Add a brief note in doc examples warning not to hardcode cosmos.mongo hostnames/ports; always use the cluster's provided connection string.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Billing is primarily RU-based (Request Units per second) for Cosmos DB accounts; no vCore-style billing for the Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute tier (vCores / M-series tiers) and storage; it is not RU-based. Compute tiers such as M30, M40, etc., and storage are billed independently.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected the RU-based Cosmos DB model used by Cosmos DB for NoSQL or Cosmos DB's Mongo RU-based offering, not the vCore-based billing used by DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.build_risk: The sample's cost guidance, cluster sizing recommendations and README would be wrong; the builder might attempt to set RUs or use autoscale APIs that don't apply.
improvements: Update any sample docs to state that Azure DocumentDB uses vCore M-series tiers and independent storage billing; include a short pricing pointer and M-tier examples.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB SCRAM (username/password) is the common method; Microsoft Entra ID integration is not generally available for the Mongo wire protocol.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) credentials and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication for clusters that enable MicrosoftEntraID auth; the cluster's allowed auth modes can include NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID (see CLI flags). The docs demonstrate Entra ID / RBAC integration for cluster-level and data-plane authentication when configured.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (azure-portal)
az documentdb mongocluster create (auth-allowed-modes)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos/Mongo offerings used only SCRAM; the newer vCore DocumentDB supports Microsoft Entra ID when configured (the CLI shows `--auth-allowed-modes` including MicrosoftEntraID).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming Entra ID is unavailable could prevent implementing a preferred secure auth method (or conversely, assuming Entra ID available without enabling it would cause connection failures).
improvements: Add a note in the sample README that DocumentDB clusters can accept NativeAuth or MicrosoftEntraID depending on the cluster configuration and that the agent should read the chosen mode from cluster configuration or instructions.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor); there is no separate Mongo-specific Azure SDK for application code.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (for Python, pymongo or motor). There is no separate runtime SDK for application-level MongoDB operations; management SDKs exist for resource control, but application code should use pymongo.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Django MongoDB backend to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect HNSW, possibly IVF and DiskANN; example createIndex: { embedding: 'vector' } with method 'hnsw' and dimensions: 1536.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann. Indexes are created via a `createIndexes` (runCommand) invocation with `key: { <path>: 'cosmosSearch' }` and `cosmosSearchOptions` that include `kind` (vector-ivf|vector-hnsw|vector-diskann), `dimensions`, `similarity`, and algorithm-specific params (m, efConstruction, numLists, maxDegree, lBuild, etc.). Vector search queries use an aggregation `$search` stage with `cosmosSearch`.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search examples)
Create a DiskANN/HNSW/IVF example

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer guessed index option names from general vector-store conventions; Azure DocumentDB uses the `cosmosSearch` key and `cosmosSearchOptions` object with `kind` values (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann) and specific parameters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the guessed MongoDB Atlas syntax (e.g., `{ embedding: 'vector' }` with different option names), index creation would fail. The sample must use the documented createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions shape.
improvements: Show a canonical `db.runCommand({ createIndexes: ..., indexes: [...] })` example for each `kind` in the sample README (use the official `cosmosSearchOptions` shape).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search normally via Azure Cognitive Search or Mongo text indexes; hybrid requires separate search service or provider-specific APIs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in BM25 full-text search via `createSearchIndexes` and the `$search` aggregation stage (BM25, fuzzy, phrase, custom analyzers). Hybrid (BM25 + vector) search is supported by creating both a search index and a vector index on the same collection and fusing the results (server-side RRF or $unionWith-based server-side fusion). No separate Azure Cognitive Search service is required for these DocumentDB-native capabilities.

grounding_links.title: Hybrid search
Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed Azure Cognitive Search or external indexing; newer integrated full-text + vector + hybrid patterns are implemented within DocumentDB's `createSearchIndexes` + `cosmosSearch` mechanisms.
confusions.build_risk: Using external Azure Cognitive Search would add unnecessary complexity and cost; the sample should use the integrated `createSearchIndexes` / `$search` + vector index approach.
improvements: Document the integrated `createSearchIndexes` workflow for BM25 and show an example RRF fusion pipeline in the sample README.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Compatibility historically depends on selected server version; need to check account (3.6, 4.x etc.).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions including 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (availability depends on the chosen serverVersion for the cluster). The service documents per-version MQL/operator compat details; a compatibility matrix is available. Some admin-level or platform-managed commands are handled by the service and some rare operators are omitted — consult the compatibility docs for exact operator availability.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged; the service explicitly publishes supported server-version families and has a `serverVersion` cluster property to choose compatibility.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a different wire protocol version than the cluster supports, driver behavior or certain operators may fail. The sample must read cluster serverVersion or document the expected minimum driver version.
improvements: In the sample README, add a check step that calls `az documentdb mongocluster show` or the MCP `listConnectionStrings` / cluster metadata to confirm serverVersion, and instruct which pymongo version to use accordingly.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB official Docker image (mongo:6.0) on port 27017; CosmosDB emulator doesn't emulate Mongo API fully.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB local gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) for local DocumentDB development; the gateway listens on port 10260 by default (TLS). The Azure DocumentDB emulator / local operator uses port 10260 and a documented local connection string format (mongodb://...@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true).

grounding_links.title: Development loop - run local DocumentDB gateway

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested fallback to plain MongoDB server; DocumentDB provides a local gateway image and explicit port (10260) for near-parity development.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain MongoDB image may not expose DocumentDB-specific features (search, vector indexes, or control-plane behaviors), leading to mismatches in sample verification.
improvements: Add a short local-dev section in the sample README showing the exact `docker run` for DocumentDB local and the local connection string (port 10260) so builders don't use plain MongoDB images by default.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams may be available depending on selected server version; historically Cosmos had change feed for SQL API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. Multi-shard (cluster-wide) change streams are a feature that can require enabling under cluster Features (e.g., 'Change streams for multishard clusters') and may be in preview for some scenarios. The docs show how to enable change-stream features and usage examples (`db.collection.watch()`), including resume tokens and historical replay.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer mixed Cosmos DB change feed history with MongoDB change streams; DocumentDB supports Mongo-style change streams and documents enabling multi-shard change streams in settings.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are always enabled cluster-wide, production code relying on cluster-wide streams might fail; sample should either use single-shard watch() or document feature enablement steps.
improvements: In the sample README indicate whether the sample uses change streams and document how to enable multi-shard change-streams feature in the portal or via CLI if the sample depends on it.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the `documentdb` MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection and tools; Azure MCP server covers control-plane only.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the `documentdb` MCP server provides the data-plane tools (list/create indexes, aggregate, explain, sample docs) for Azure DocumentDB. The general Azure MCP server is present for control-plane tasks but the documentdb server gives the agent direct cluster inspection and query abilities.
confusions.grounding_source: (inventory) documentdb MCP server tools listed in the machine inventory

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally named an internal NoSQL service DocumentDB; that platform evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB (Mongo API) is Microsoft's managed wire-protocol-compatible service; it is not the same as open-source DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: The product history is nuanced: Azure DocumentDB (the current vCore offering) was formerly known internally as vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'; the name 'DocumentDB' has been used historically and refers now to this vCore managed MongoDB-compatible offering built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. It is distinct from the older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts-based offering (the RU model) and distinct from Amazon DocumentDB. The open-source DocumentDB engine (documentdb repo) is the upstream engine that powers the Azure DocumentDB service.

grounding_links.title: Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical naming overlap (DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, and 'vCore' labels) causes frequent confusion; the cold answer conflated multiple historical names.
confusions.build_risk: Using an older 'Cosmos DB databaseAccounts' mental model will lead to incorrect resources and APIs; the sample must use the vCore DocumentDB APIs.
improvements: Add a single concise 'Product relationship' paragraph in the sample README clarifying: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) ≠ Cosmos DB (RU) databaseAccounts, and that DocumentDB is vCore-based and built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s proprietary Cosmos DB engine; applications should use standard MongoDB drivers but expect differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Under the vCore offering Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (documentdb repo). Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) and expect generally compatible behavior, but must validate specific operators and features against the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer assumed the 'Cosmos DB engine' branding; in fact the vCore service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine which may affect local dev choices and licensing considerations.
confusions.build_risk: Misunderstanding engine provenance could lead to incorrect expectations about local runtimes, licensing, and which features are available locally.
improvements: Add a clear line in the sample README: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) runs the open-source DocumentDB engine (MIT) — local development uses the official DocumentDB gateway image.'

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?

confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the sample run environment explicitly requires using the database sample_banking_11.

confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo. Example: MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True) and db = client['sample_banking_11'].
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use pymongo (the standard MongoDB Python driver). The quickstarts and tutorials reference PyMongo for Python examples; the sample should follow the documentdb-driver skill guidance (singleton MongoClient pattern) and read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env.

confusions.question: What index definition will I create for vector search in this sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field using createIndex with cosmosSearch or a vector key and options (example given with method 'hnsw' and dimensions 1536).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the `createIndexes` runCommand with the `key` mapping to `"cosmosSearch"` and a `cosmosSearchOptions` object specifying `kind` (vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann), `dimensions`, `similarity`, and algorithm params. The sample must choose `dimensions` to match the chosen embedding model (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3-small -> 1536 dims) and select `kind` appropriate to dataset/cluster tier (DiskANN or HNSW for M30+).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (createIndexes and cosmosSearchOptions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer had the right idea (HNSW) but used guessed driver syntax rather than the documented `cosmosSearchOptions` runCommand shape.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses incorrect index creation syntax, index creation will fail; the sample should use the documented JSON runCommand shape.
improvements: Include an explicit `db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'correspondents', indexes:[{ name: ..., key:{ '<path>':'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: <n>, ... } }]})` example in the sample code and README.

confusions.question: Which port and TLS options will the sample expect in the connection string?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect TLS over port 10255 and require ssl=true (or tls=true).
confusions.grounded_answer: Do not hardcode port/host: use the cluster-provided connection string (via az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal). Local gateway uses port 10260 (tls=true & tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true). The cloud cluster will return the SCRAM-SHA-256 connection strings (often in SRV form), so the sample should accept and use the cluster-provided string and set TLS as directed by it.

Development loop - DocumentDB local gateway (port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the older Cosmos DB Mongo port 10255; vCore clusters and SRV strings differ; the sample must rely on the supplied connection string.
confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding an incorrect port or TLS options may cause connection failures; the sample must use the env DOCUMENTDB_URI or fetch the cluster's connection strings to ensure correct options.
improvements: Add a line to the sample README that instructs the user to copy the exact connection string from the portal or `az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings` into the `.env` as DOCUMENTDB_URI and never to hardcode host/port.

confusions.question: How will I perform vector search queries from the application (aggregation stage / command)?
confusions.cold_answer: Use an aggregation-stage style vector search exposed by the provider, example `$vectorSearch` stage or fallback to provider-specific find; use $search with cosmosSearch if available.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the aggregation `$search` stage with the `cosmosSearch` operator and provide the query vector, `path`, `k`, and algorithm-specific params (efSearch, lSearch, etc.). The documented pattern is an aggregation pipeline where `$search: { cosmosSearch: { vector: <vec>, path: '<path>', k: <n>, ... } }` is the first stage, with downstream `$project` to capture `$meta: "searchScore"`.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (perform vector search example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested a `$vectorSearch` stage (Atlas/other variants); DocumentDB uses `$search` + `cosmosSearch` operator in the aggregation pipeline.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Atlas-specific `$vectorSearch` syntax or a mismatched aggregation stage, queries would fail; must use documented `$search`/`cosmosSearch` syntax.
improvements: Add the exact `$search` + `cosmosSearch` aggregation example to the sample code and tests, including projection of `searchScore`.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the resource type for vCore DocumentDB clusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
Use the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / list-connection-strings) for cluster management and to retrieve authoritative connection strings.

Create vector indexes using db.runCommand(createIndexes) with key set to 'cosmosSearch' and a `cosmosSearchOptions` object specifying `kind` (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann), `dimensions`, and algorithm-specific parameters; query with `$search` + `cosmosSearch` and project `$meta: 'searchScore'`.

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Enable and use the built-in full-text search (createSearchIndexes + $search) and perform hybrid BM25+vector fusion with server-side RRF or $unionWith; do not rely on an external Cognitive Search service for hybrid retrieval in this sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample: the prompt explicitly uses an existing cluster (no provisioning via azd). Do not install unless you plan to add azd-based CI/CD scaffolding.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not strictly required for building the sample (the cluster is pre-provisioned). If you plan to add an optional IaC example, install Bicep (`az bicep install`) or include a Bicep fragment that uses the mongoClusters resource.

references.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the sample run (no provisioning). If adding Terraform examples, use the AzAPI provider targeting microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters; otherwise omit.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python sample. Add only if adding .NET sample variants.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for interactive cluster inspection and quick manual verification (e.g., `npm install -g mongosh` or use your OS package manager). Workaround: use the documentdb MCP server or small pymongo scripts to run the same checks if mongosh cannot be installed.
